title: Fixed #29504 -- Documented limitations of integer-like keys in JSONField.
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-29504

#### Branch description

This PR updates `docs/topics/db/queries.txt` to document the limitations of querying `JSONField` dictionaries that have integer-like keys (e.g. `{"0": "value"}`). It clarifies that integer keys are interpreted as array index transforms, meaning queries like `data__0="value"` do not match dictionary keys, and notes that chained lookups (`data__0__nested`) only work on PostgreSQL and are not portable across databases.

title: Fixed #33586 -- Made RunPython reload delayed models when unapplying.
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-33586

#### Branch description

`RunPython.database_forwards()` calls `from_state.clear_delayed_apps_cache()` before running `code`, but `database_backwards()` didn't do the same before running `reverse_code`. As a result, `reverse_code` could receive stale related models after an applied migration, which wasn't being unapplied, reloaded a model with `delay=True`. This makes the backwards path match the forwards path and the requirement documented for custom operations in `docs/ref/migration-operations.txt`.

The fix follows the approach discussed on the ticket. It keeps the delayed-reload optimization from #27666 rather than making `_find_reload_model()` recursive, which benchmarked roughly 25x slower per reload at 1000 models.

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) was used throughout. While I was working on another project, it diagnosed the root cause of the stale related models seen there. In this repository it wrote the analysis and benchmark that I posted on the ticket, wrote the regression test and the fix, and drafted this description. I reviewed all changes and ran the test suite locally.

title: Fixed #37401 -- Used os.makedirs() for safe_makedirs() on Python 3.15+.
body:
#### Trac ticket number
<!-- Replace XXXXX with the corresponding Trac ticket number. -->
<!-- Or delete the line and write "N/A - typo" for typo fixes. -->

ticket-37401

#### Branch description

Python 3.15 added the `parent_mode` argument to `os.makedirs()`, the upstream fix for the issue that led Django to vendor its own `makedirs()` in the fix for CVE-2026-25674. The vendored copy differed from CPython only by an extra `chmod()` call that ignored the process umask. Adopting the standard library semantics allows relying on `os.makedirs()` directly, and dropping the vendored copy once Python 3.14 support ends.

As a result, directories created by `FileSystemStorage` when `FILE_UPLOAD_DIRECTORY_PERMISSIONS` (or `directory_permissions_mode`) is set, and by `FileBasedCache`, now have the requested mode combined with the process umask, and the set-group-ID bit and other bits beyond the last 9 are no longer explicitly set.

Thanks Shai Berger for the proposal, and Ken Whitesell, Tim Schilling, and Carlton Gibson for the discussion.

title: Fixed #19649 -- Added Vary: Cookie for cookie message reads.
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-19649

#### Branch description

The longstanding accepted ticket describes how a response using cookie-backed messages can be reused across clients by a shared cache when it lacks `Vary: Cookie`. I reproduced that behavior against the current `main` branch with two clients and Django's site-wide cache middleware.

This resubmits #22084 with the same commit after claiming the Trac ticket as `shin4141`. GitHub did not allow reopening the bot-closed original PR.

This change records when `CookieStorage` reads the request cookie and adds `Cookie` to `Vary` in `MessageMiddleware`'s response phase. It also covers `FallbackStorage`, which uses `CookieStorage` internally. It leaves general `request.COOKIES` tracking and the other middleware unchanged.

The rule is deliberately conservative: a response varies on `Cookie` after a storage read even if the view discards the value. That can reduce shared-cache reuse across different Cookie headers. Responses that never read cookie message storage retain their existing cache behavior. This follows the accessed-state approach used by `SessionMiddleware` without extending the older framework-wide proposal.

The regression tests cover A-to-B cache reuse on unmodified `main` and its absence after this fix, the empty-cookie client first, non-iterating message reads, a read whose result is ignored, delayed template rendering, existing `Vary` headers, and interactions with session storage, fallback storage, CSRF, and the cache middleware.

Verification: On Python 3.12 in an offline container, Django's `messages_tests` and `cache` suites passed (817 tests, 209 skipped). Black 26.5.1, isort 8.0.1, flake8 7.3.0, and `git diff --check` passed. A Sphinx dummy build completed; offline intersphinx lookups produced warnings unrelated to the changed paragraph.

title: Added CSP nonce-fallback check (security.W028) and COOP noopener-allow-popups value

labels.name: no ticket
labels.description: Based on PR title, no linked Trac ticket

body:
### Summary

Two related hardening changes to `django/core/checks/security/base.py`.

**1. New `security.W028` — a nonce-only CSP directive silently fails open.**

In `django.utils.csp.build_policy()`, when a directive's only source is `CSP.NONCE` and the
per-request nonce was never accessed (the `LazyNonce` stays falsy because the response rendered no
`{{ csp_nonce }}`), the sentinel is stripped, the directive becomes empty, and the directive is
**dropped from the header entirely**. For the same config, the emitted policy then depends on
whether the nonce happened to be used:

| `SECURE_CSP` | nonce used | nonce **unused** |
|---|---|---|
| `{"default-src": ["*"], "script-src": [CSP.NONCE]}` | `default-src *; script-src 'nonce-…'` | `default-src *` — `script-src` gone, scripts fall back to `*` |
| `{"script-src": [CSP.NONCE]}` | `script-src 'nonce-…'` | `""` — empty header, no policy at all |
| `{"script-src": [CSP.SELF, CSP.NONCE]}` (recommended) | … | `script-src 'self'` — fails **closed**, unaffected |

So a nonce-only directive silently degrades to its `default-src` fallback (possibly permissive) or
to no CSP, on exactly the responses most likely to carry injected markup (error pages, views with
no inline nonce'd element). The recommended form — pairing `CSP.NONCE` with an explicit fallback —
already fails closed and is unaffected.

This adds a system check, `security.W028`, that warns when any `SECURE_CSP` /
`SECURE_CSP_REPORT_ONLY` directive's only source is `CSP.NONCE`, hinting to add `CSP.SELF`,
`CSP.STRICT_DYNAMIC`, or `CSP.NONE`. It mirrors the existing `security.W027`. No runtime behavior
changes.

**2. Accept the `noopener-allow-popups` COOP value.**

`check_cross_origin_opener_policy` rejected `SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY =
"noopener-allow-popups"` with `security.E024`, even though it is a standards-track
`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` value (supported by Chrome and Safari) that severs the opener
relationship even for same-origin popups — stronger isolation than `same-origin-allow-popups`.
Setting this valid, more-hardened value therefore broke `manage.py check --deploy`. This adds it to
`CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY_VALUES`.

### Testing

- New `CheckCspNonceWithoutFallbackTests` and an added value in `CheckCrossOriginOpenerPolicyTest.test_with_coop`.
- Full test suite passes locally (`runtests.py`, 19,887 tests OK); `black`/`isort`/`flake8` clean.
- Docs added: `checks.txt` (W028), `middleware.txt` (COOP value, `versionadded:: 6.2`), `releases/6.2.txt`.

### Notes

- Happy to split into two commits, or to file a Trac ticket if preferred.

#### Branch description

The main issue was applying old migrations of models that inherit but are unmanaged. A prime example is a database view that extends a real model, both in terms of python functions and with database columns.

The `model.py` is as follows:
```python
from django.db import models

class Parent(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField()

class Child(Parent):
    class Meta:
        managed = False
```

The main culprit happened, when the `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` setting changed e.g. from `django.db.models.AutoField` to `BigAutoField`. This lead `makemigrations` to create an operation:

```python
migrations.AlterField(
            model_name='parent',
            name='id',
            field=models.AutoField(auto_created=True, primary_key=True, serialize=False, verbose_name='ID'),
        ),
```

This migration in the current code tried to follow the parent_ptr OneToOne relation and update the foreign key in the Child table. As Child is a view, this failed on postgres.
The proposed fix is to exclude unmanaged models in the `_is_relevant_relation` function to make old migrations run.

body:

#### Branch description
`UnorderedObjectListWarning` used a fixed `stacklevel=3`. That level is only correct when `Paginator` is instantiated directly. #### Trac ticket number

`identify_hasher()` passed a hash’s algorithm prefix directly to `get_hasher()`. title: Fixed #37376 -- Made UUID4() persist data in lowercase on Oracle.
body:
#### Trac ticket number
ticket-37376

#### Branch description
On Oracle, UUID4() produces a RAW(16) value. Because Django uses VARCHAR2(32) for UUIDField(), Oracle implicitly ran RAWTOHEX() when inserting, producing uppercased values. Lookups then failed as all other value preparation by UUIDField produces lowercased values.

Making get_db_prep_value() normalize values to uppercase on Oracle was rejected, as it would break too many existing uses without the new UUID4() function.

title: Fixed #37352 -- Supported server_time with all logging format styles.
body:
#### Trac ticket number
ticket-37352

#### Branch description
`django.utils.log.ServerFormatter` assumed format strings always used brace-style (`{`) formatting when determining whether to add `server_time` to a `LogRecord`. This caused logging configurations using percent-style (`%`) or template-style (`$`) formatters to omit `server_time`.

This patch updates `ServerFormatter` to inspect the formatter's active logging style class rather than guessing from string contents:
- **Brace style (`{`):** Detects `{server_time}` while handling nested format specifications and attribute/item lookups (including keys with dots).
- **Percent style (`%`):** Recognizes valid `%(server_time)` conversion directives while ignoring escaped percent signs (`%%`).
- **Template style (`$`):** Distinguishes real placeholders (`$server_time`, `${server_time}`) from escaped delimiters (`$$`).
- Preserves caller-supplied `server_time` values already set on records and retains standard Python logging errors for malformed or unrelated format strings.

Regression tests were added to `tests/logging_tests/tests.py` covering all three format styles, escaped placeholders, nested specs/lookups, formats without `server_time`, pre-existing record attributes, and malformed string error handling.

title: Fixed #37377 -- Fixed JSONField __in crash/incorrect results for bare Value() primitives.
body:
#### Trac ticket number
<!-- Replace XXXXX with the corresponding Trac ticket number. -->
<!-- Or delete the line and write "N/A - typo" for typo fixes. -->

ticket-37377

#### Branch description
<!-- Provide a concise overview of the issue or rationale behind the proposed changes. Minimum five words. -->

Refs ticket-36689. 9b8e4c6d7d wrapped every `Value()` rhs `param` of a `JSONIn` lookup in `JSON_EXTRACT()`/`JSON_VALUE()` on assuming it was already JSON-serialized. That only holds for `Value(..., JSONField())`; a bare `Value("primitive")` gets an inferred non-JSON `output_field` (e.g. `CharField`), so its compiled param was a raw primitive, not JSON text. Wrapping that raw text produced malformed JSON on SQLite and wrong results on MariaDB.

`JSONIn.resolve_expression_parameter()` now JSON-encodes the `Value`'s raw `.value` itself whenever its `output_field` isn't `JSONField`, instead of trusting whatever its inferred `output_field` produced.

As a side effect, this also fixes `Value(True)/Value(False)` in `__in`, which were previously compared as raw Python bools against the JSON-extracted `lhs` and never matched.

title: Fixed #37379 -- Made migrate check for the django_migrations table once.
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37379

#### Branch description
Replaces #22047, which was auto-closed before the ticket was assigned.

MigrationRecorder.has_table() looked for django_migrations by listing every table. On PostgreSQL that means a pg_class seq scan with pg_table_is_visible() on each row. On our database (~1,500 schemas, 5.2M pg_class rows) that took 1.3–3.5 s per call, and one migrate did it three times because the loader, the consistency check and the executor each had their own recorder. Filtering with c.relname = ANY(%s) turns it into an index scan, about 8 ms on the same catalog.

Three commits, as suggested on the ticket:

1. Adds table_names(only_tables=...) plus a get_table_list_for_names() hook that the built-in backends implement to filter in SQL. The default filters get_table_list() in Python. If a subclass overrides get_table_list() but not the new hook, table_names() keeps using their get_table_list() (django-tenants does this to pin the search path), so existing subclasses don't silently change behaviour.
2. Uses it in has_table(), createcachetable, django_table_names(only_existing=True) and a few test helpers. I left SchemaTests.delete_tables() and MigrationExecutor.detect_soft_applied() on the full table list, since they lowercase names when ignores_table_name_case is set and an exact-name filter would change that.
3. Shares the loader's recorder with check_consistent_history() and MigrationExecutor, so migrate checks once.

Open questions:
- Is the check for an overridden get_table_list() ok, or would you rather just document it in the release notes?
- django_table_names(only_existing=True) is on the flush path. Happy to drop it from this PR if you'd rather keep the change small.

Not run locally: MySQL, Oracle, GIS backends.

title: Fixed #36279 -- Made translate_url() handle unnamed URL patterns.
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-36279

#### Branch description

`translate_url()` builds the name to reverse from `match.url_name`, so a translated pattern without a `name` (or an unnamed pattern inside a namespaced `include()`, which ends up as `"account:None"`) is never translated and `set_language()` redirects to a 404.

Reversing by the view callable, as in the earlier PR #19327, is ambiguous: when the same view is used by several unnamed patterns (as in `tests/i18n/patterns/urls/default.py`, where one `view` serves every pattern), `reverse(match.func)` picks whichever candidate comes first and silently returns a different URL. This PR instead reverses the exact pattern that matched: the last entry of `match.tried` is the chain of resolvers ending with the matching `URLPattern`, so a throwaway resolver tree containing only that chain is built and the view is reversed against it. Named patterns keep the existing code path.

Tests use the case from comment:2 on the ticket, with the unnamed pattern placed between named ones so that the test also fails with the reverse-by-callable approach (it returns `/nl/gebruikers/`), plus an unnamed pattern inside the namespaced include.

One design note for reviewers: this relies on `match.tried[-1]` being the successful chain, which `URLResolver.resolve()` guarantees but the docs for `tried` don't spell out. If you'd rather have an explicit attribute on `ResolverMatch`, I'm happy to change the approach.

`_SEP_UNSAFE` in `django/core/signing.py` uses the character class `[A-z0-9-_=]`. The `A-z` range is the classic ASCII-range regex typo: it spans `A` (0x41) through `z` (0x7A) inclusive, which sweeps in six punctuation characters that sit between `Z` and `a` in ASCII (`[ \ ] ^ _` `` ` ``) in addition to the intended `A-Z` and `a-z`.

```pycon
>>> import re
>>> p = re.compile(r'^[A-z0-9-_=]*$')
>>> p.match('^')   # True -- should be False, '^' is not in A-Za-z0-9-_=
>>> p.match('{')   # False -- correctly rejected

This regex is used to reject "unsafe" sep values passed to Signer/TimestampSigner. The typo only makes the rejected set larger than the documented rule, not smaller — it fails safe. It's not a security issue, just an incorrect validation: a handful of legitimate separator choices (e.g. sep="^") are wrongly rejected with a ValueError.

Fix:

_SEP_UNSAFE = _lazy_re_compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9-_=]*$")

Also updates the corresponding ValueError message text (which repeated the same A-z0-9-_= typo), adds a regression test covering the previously-misrejected characters, and clarifies the docs wording for sep to mention the = padding character.

Tested via tests/signing/tests.py (21/21 passing, including the new test_sep_excluded_ascii_range).

title: Fixed #36833 -- Made split_header_value() respect quoted strings.
body:
Ticket: #36833

## Problem
`django.utils.http.split_header_value` blindly splits string values on commas, even if those commas are enclosed within double quotes. This causes HTTP headers with quoted comma-separated values (such as `Accept` headers generated by some clients) to be improperly split into broken, partial tokens, failing content negotiation or producing incorrect parsing results.

## Root Cause
The previous implementation used a simple regex or `.split(',')`, ignoring RFC HTTP quoted string semantics. 

## Solution
Modified `split_header_value` to use a parsing pattern similar to Django's `_parseparam`, leveraging a state-aware while-loop that tracks double quotes and backslash escaping. It correctly yields values split by *unquoted* commas only. 

## Testing
Added `test_accept_headers_with_quoted_comma` to `tests.requests_tests.test_accept_header` and verified correctness against existing regression suite.

title: Fixed #37362 -- Raised ValueError for encoded hashes whose algorithm segment is the literal string "default"
body:
#### Trac ticket number

ticket-37362

#### Branch description

Fixes a sentinel collision in `identify_hasher()`. When a stored password hash's algorithm segment is the literal string `"default"` (e.g. `default$$$$`), the old code handed that string to `get_hasher()`, where it matched the `"default"` sentinel and returned the first configured hasher instead of being treated as an unknown algorithm. The mismatched hasher then failed in `decode()` with a bare `AssertionError`, rather than the `ValueError` that `identify_hasher()`'s docstring promises. This is reachable through `check_password()`, the exact function `User.check_password()` and `ModelBackend.authenticate()` call on every login attempt.

The fix looks the algorithm up in `get_hashers_by_algorithm()` directly, so any unrecognized name (including the literal `"default"`) raises `ValueError("Unknown password hashing algorithm ...")` as documented, and `check_password()` fails closed by returning `False`. The public `get_hasher("default")` sentinel behavior is unchanged.

Reproduction (on `main` before the fix):

```python
import django
from django.conf import settings
settings.configure(
    SECRET_KEY="x",
    PASSWORD_HASHERS=["django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher"],
)
django.setup()
from django.contrib.auth.hashers import check_password
check_password("some guess", "default$$$$")  # raised bare AssertionError
```

After the fix, that call returns `False`, and `identify_hasher("default$$$$")` raises `ValueError: Unknown password hashing algorithm 'default'. Did you specify it in the PASSWORD_HASHERS setting?`

Tests: added `test_default_algorithm_sentinel_collision` to `tests/auth_tests/test_hashers.py` covering both `identify_hasher()` and `check_password()`. Ran the full `auth_tests.test_hashers` suite (SQLite): all tests pass.

title: Fixed #37225 -- Prevented file_move_safe() from overwriting concurren…
body:
…tly created destination when allow_overwrite=False.

#### Trac ticket number
<!-- Replace XXXXX with the corresponding Trac ticket number. -->
<!-- Or delete the line and write "N/A - typo" for typo fixes. -->

ticket-37225

#### Branch description
When `allow_overwrite=False`, `django.core.files.move.file_move_safe()` previously checked whether the destination existed with `os.access()` before calling `os.rename()`. On POSIX systems, `os.rename()` atomically replaces an existing destination file, introducing a race condition where a destination created between `os.access()` and `os.rename()` was silently overwritten.



This PR addresses the issue by:
1. Using `os.link()` and `os.unlink()` instead of `os.rename()` when `allow_overwrite=False`. `os.link()` atomically fails with `FileExistsError` if the destination exists, preventing overwrite.
2. In the fallback chunked copy path, wrapping `os.open(..., os.O_EXCL)` in `try...except FileExistsError:` to provide the consistent error message (`Destination file <name> exists and allow_overwrite is False.`).
3. Adding tests in `tests/files/tests.py` covering both the primary `os.link()` path and the cross-filesystem fallback path.
